 Five things I check on a launch directory before I pay for its premium slot 
Disclosure first, since it matters for this one: I run a few launch sites myself, and they sell paid slots too. So I've seen this from both sides, and I still think most founders buy the upgrade too fast. It's usually $15 to $50, it's late at night before a launch, and the button says "skip the queue". Before I pay any directory now, mine included, I check five things.
 1. The rel attribute on a live paid listing. Not the pricing page, not the FAQ. Open someone else's premium listing, view source, find the link to their site. If it says nofollow or sponsored, that's the deal, whatever the marketing copy says. Our own dofollow link checker does this in a few seconds if you don't feel like reading HTML.
 2. Whether the listing page is even indexed. Search site: plus the directory domain plus a product name from last month. A dofollow link on a page Google never picked up doesn't do much.
 3. What "featured" actually means and for how long. One day on the home page and seven days in a sidebar are very different purchases. If they don't say, ask. If they won't answer, that's an answer.
 4. Whether last week's paid launches got any comments. Upvotes are easy to inflate. Real comments from people who aren't the maker are harder, and they tell you if anyone reads the site.
 5. What I'm actually buying: a date, a link, or eyeballs. Most of the time I'm paying to pick my launch date and skip a queue. That's fine! I just want to know that's what it is before I expect traffic from it.
 None of this takes more than ten minutes, and it's the difference between buying a backlink and buying a nicer badge. If you want a wider list of where to launch when you're bootstrapped, I keep notes on launch platforms that make sense for bootstrapped founders .

 14 of our articles were telling Google they were copies of the homepage, because of one line I never wrote 
Last week I found a bug that had been sitting quietly on three of our launch sites, EarlyHunt, MakerHunt and SideHunt. Every article under /posts had a canonical tag pointing at the homepage. So 14 articles were basically telling Google "I'm just a copy of the homepage, you can ignore me".
 Nobody wrote that on purpose. The canonical was set in the Next.js root layout, and every route that doesn't override it just inherits it. The pages looked totally fine in the browser. Nothing broke, no error, nothing in the logs. You only see it if you view source. We fixed it on Oct 21 and each article now points at itself. I can't tell you yet if it changed anything in search, it's way too early, I'll look in Search Console in a few weeks.
 What bugged me more is how easy this is to miss. So I built a small free check for it on Aura++, and while testing it a few things surprised me:
 example.com doesn't declare a canonical at all. Not exactly wrong, but I expected the most famous test page on the internet to have one.
github.com does it the textbook way. One absolute canonical pointing at itself, og:url matches it, and the target returns 200.
A canonical can live in two places. The HTML head, or an HTTP Link header. If you only grep the HTML you can miss the second one.
A canonical pointing at a 404 or a redirect kind of cancels itself. So it's worth checking what the target actually returns, not just that the tag exists.
If you want to check one of your own pages, the free canonical tag checker on Aura++ takes a URL and tells you if there's a canonical, if it points at itself, how it compares with og:url and if the target returns 200. No signup. Or honestly just run curl on a deep page and grep for canonical, thats how I found ours.
 My rule now: any time I add a layout or template that sets metadata, I open one deep page, not the homepage, and check the canonical before I call it done.

 Four rules I wrote down before the second customer asked to pause instead of cancel 
A pause request is one of the nicer support emails you can get. The person isn't leaving. They just don't want to pay for months they won't use. Think a tool for wedding photographers, and in November someone writes "season's done, can I pause till March, I don't want to lose my setup".
 The first time I looked at this in Stripe I found two different things called pause, and they do very different stuff. Pausing payment collection keeps the subscription active, keeps creating invoices, and the person keeps access. It's really a grace period. The newer "pause subscription" (Stripe added on-demand pause and resume in their changelog on Sep 30) changes the status to paused and stops invoices completely. Use the wrong one and you either quietly bill someone all winter or you lock out someone who only wanted a break.
 So under 50 customers my take is: don't wing it per email. Write a tiny policy once. Mine is four rules.
 "Away" and "can't pay" are different requests. Not using it gets a real pause. Still using it but money is tight gets paused collection, and I decide up front if I'm forgiving those months or they pay later.
Every pause has an end date. Max three months. "Until you resume it" is how a pause turns into an account nobody remembers, using the product free for a year.
Paused means read-only, nothing deleted. They can log in, look, export. I say that in the reply so they're not anxious about their data.
I email them a few days before it resumes. I didn't see anything in Stripe's pause docs about Stripe emailing the customer before a resume, so I put a reminder in my calendar and send a short "you're back on March 1, here's what you'll pay" note. Also if they had a discount, it keeps counting down during the pause, which I mention.
The reply then is boring in a good way: "Sure, paused from today until March 1. No charge before then, your projects stay as they are and you can still log in. First charge in March will be a bit lower because of the unused days this month. I'll email you before."
 Pause is for "not right now", cancel is for "not for me", and I keep them as two separate buttons in my head.
 The longer version with the Stripe fields, the cases where the pause button is greyed out, and what your paywall should check is in my write-up on handling a pause request with under 50 customers .

 Is your launch link a 301 or a 302? I check it before I submit it anywhere now 
Small admission first. The URL I paste into a launch form is usually just whatever is in my address bar. I'd never properly looked at what happens between someone clicking it and the page loading. Could be one hop, could be four.
 So this week I shipped a small free tool on Aura++ for exactly that, and the rule I'm keeping now is simple: before a URL goes into any submit form, I paste it in and look at every hop.
 Why I think it matters, in plain words:
 a 302 says "temporary". If you moved your site for good, from http to https, or from an old domain to a new one, that should be a 301. With a 302 you're telling Google the old URL is still the real one, so the old address can hang around in results longer than you want. It's easy to set a redirect in a hosting panel or plugin and never really choose which one you got.
every hop is a round trip. A visitor from a launch board is impatient already. Two or three extra hops before the first byte of your page isn't great, specially on mobile.
chains and loops grow quietly. You add https, then www, then a new homepage path, and each rule was fine on its own day.
Worked example from the real tests we ran while building it. Typing http://github.com gives one 301 to https://github.com/ in 17 ms, then a 200. That's the clean version, one permanent hop and done. A test URL we set up to return a 302 goes to https://example.com and then 200. Same result for a visitor, the page loads, but the second one is telling search engines "don't update anything, this is temporary".
 Now picture the common indie setup, as an example not a real site: http://yoursite.com goes to https://yoursite.com, then to https://www.yoursite.com, then to /home. That's three hops before anything useful. If one of them is a 302 left over from testing, you'd never notice in the browser. You'd only see it if you look at each status code.
 What the tool shows: every hop with its status code, the Location header and the time it took. It flags 301 vs 302, loops and long chains. Free, no signup. One thing it won't do on purpose: it refuses private and internal addresses like 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254, so you can't use it to poke at someone's internal network.
 If you want to check the link you're about to submit somewhere, it's the free redirect checker on Aura++ . Takes about ten seconds.
 What I still don't know is how common this is out there. When you launch, do you submit your bare domain, the www version, or a specific landing page? And have you ever actually looked at what it redirects through?

 Should "delete my account" be as easy to find as "upgrade"? I think it should 
Here's a small test I like doing on any SaaS I sign up for, including my own. Open settings and try to find how to delete the account. Not cancel the plan, delete the whole thing, data and all. Time how long it takes.
 On a lot of small products the answer is "you can't, email us". Or there's a link buried three screens deep under Advanced. I get why founders do it. Nobody wants to build the button that makes users disappear. But I think hiding it costs more trust than it saves users.
 My rule now: the delete option sits on the same settings page as billing, it's visible without scrolling much, and it says plainly what happens.
 Why I think this matters before you have many users:
 people check before they sign up, not after. Someone careful about their data will look for an exit before they paste anything real in. If they can't find one, some of them just don't start.
"email us to delete" reads like a trap, even when it isn't. It suggests someone will try to talk them out of it.
it's partly not optional anyway. If you have an iOS app with account creation, Apple has required in-app account deletion since mid 2022. And if you have users in the EU they already have a right to ask for erasure, so you're doing the work either way, the button just makes it self-serve.
Worked example, framed as an example. Say you run a small invoicing tool. A decent delete section could be:
 one line: "Deleting removes your clients, invoices and uploads. Paid invoices you already sent stay with the people you sent them to."
a "download everything first" button that gives a CSV or zip, right above the delete button
if there's an active subscription, say clearly it stops renewing today and what happens to the time already paid for
a confirm step where they type the account email, not a guilt screen with a sad face
an email afterwards that says it's done and when backups age out, so they're not left wondering
What I'd skip: the "are you SURE? you'll lose everything!!" modal, a 30 day "we'll keep it just in case" that nobody asked for (unless you say so up front and let them skip it), and a survey they have to fill before the button works. One optional question is fine.
 The odd thing is how this changes the rest of the product. Once leaving is easy, you stop relying on friction to keep people and you have to rely on the product being worth staying for. That's uncomfortable, and probably healthy.
 It's the same idea as a fair cancel flow, which I wrote up longer in how to design a SaaS cancel flow without dark patterns . Delete is just the step after cancel that most of us forget to design at all.
 Genuine question though: does an easy delete button make you more likely to try a new tool, or do you never even look for it?

 Our own backlink spreadsheet was wrong about which directory links were dofollow 
Small admission. We keep a spreadsheet of the directories and launch sites where our products are listed, with a column for "dofollow / nofollow". I assumed that column was right.
 On Tuesday I ran our own listings through the dofollow link checker we shipped on Aura++ last week, and the spreadsheet was wrong in a way I didn't expect.
 What it actually found, on three real listings:
 SaaSHub: 3 links to Aura++ on the one page. The main "Visit website" link has no rel at all, so it's dofollow. The "Official pricing" and "Blog" links are nofollow. Our spreadsheet had SaaSHub down as nofollow.
PeerPush: 1 link, and the only thing on it is rel="noopener". That's a security thing for new tabs, it has no SEO meaning. So that one is dofollow too.
BetaList (our SideHunt listing): 0 links to sidehunt.io in the server HTML. The buttons go through a redirect on BetaList's own domain, so there's no direct link to us on that page at all, follow or not.
So the lesson for me is that "is this directory dofollow" is the wrong question. One page can have a dofollow link and two nofollow ones next to it, and some buttons that look like links to you never point at your domain.
 Couple of things I learned while building it, in case they save someone a search:
 there's no such thing as rel="dofollow". A link is dofollow when it doesn't say nofollow, ugc or sponsored

 Three things I tell closed beta users before the free part ends, and the price is the first one 
The worst way to end a free beta is an email on a Monday that says "thanks for helping, it's $29 a month from Friday". The product didn't change. The deal did, and nobody was told it was coming. That's what makes it feel like a bait and switch, not the price itself.
 So now I tell beta users three things, early and plainly.
 1. The price, in the first email, even if it's a guess. "This will probably be around $19 a month when it's out of beta" is way better than silence. People can decide if they're the kind of user who'll pay that, and the ones who aren't stop expecting free forever. If the number changes later, I just say it changed and why.
 2. The end date, or the condition that ends it. Either "free until March 1" or "free until the core workflow is stable and onboarding works without me on a call". Then about two weeks before it ends, a personal note, not a banner. A countdown bar in the app reads like pressure. A short email from the founder reads like a heads up.
 3. What happens if they don't pay. Can they export their data? Do they keep read only access for a bit? Can they still send feedback? Saying "you won't lose anything you made here" removes most of the fear, and honestly it costs almost nothing to offer.
 The people I'd ask first aren't the ones who said nice things in a call. It's the ones who used the main feature more than once in the last two weeks, invited a teammate, or emailed about a missing export because a real job depended on it. That's buying behaviour.

When I start something B2B, I want a few real companies using it while I build. Design partners, basically. The trap I keep seeing is that "design partner" quietly turns into "free user who gives feedback when they feel like it". So I keep two numbers fixed.
 Five, max. Every partner needs real founder time: a kickoff where I watch how they work today, regular calls, follow ups on what they asked for. As a solo founder I can't do that properly for more than five. Common Paper says most startups start with five or fewer, and a16z warns against going past 20 just because inbound looks good. Past five I stop learning and start doing support.
 A price, said out loud before we start. Free during the program is fine, a small paid pilot is fine, free now and a written discount later is fine. What isn't fine is "we'll figure out pricing later". If the price after the program isn't in the agreement, the last call becomes an awkward negotiation instead of a yes or no. And around halfway I ask straight up: "at the price we agreed, would you keep it?" A hesitant yes tells me a lot.
 The price also filters people. Someone who says "sure, I'd pay that if it solves X" behaves differently on calls than someone who just likes trying new tools. They show up, they bring the messy real cases, they tell me when something is useless.
 One thing I track is how many partners hit the same problem. One partner asking for something is a request. Three of five asking is the roadmap. That count stops me from building the product for whoever talks the loudest.
 And if none of the five would pay at the end, I try not to explain it away. It usually means the problem isn't painful enough, I picked the wrong kind of company, or the product isn't there yet. All three are cheaper to learn with five companies than after a launch.

 Three things that have to be true before I ask an early user for an intro 
A warm intro from an early user is probably the best lead you can get at the start. Someone who uses your thing tells a friend "this helped me", and the friend actually listens. But asking too early makes it awkward for both of you, so I wait until three things are true.
 1. They've used it for real at least three times. Not signed up, not clicked around once. Three sessions where they did the thing the product is for. Before that they don't have a story to tell, and I'd be asking them to vouch for something they haven't really tried.
 2. They said something nice without me asking. A reply like "this saved me an hour" or "my cofounder liked it". If I have to fish for the compliment first, the intro would be a favour, not a recommendation, and the other person can feel the difference.
 3. I've fixed at least one thing they reported. This one is underrated imo. Once someone has seen you listen and actually ship the fix, they trust you with their friends. Before that you're a stranger with a beta.
 When all three are true the ask is small and specific. Something like: "You mentioned the export thing last week. Is there one person you know with the same problem? When you're trying to get your first 20 or 30 people into early access, it's really tempting to promise stuff. Someone is on the fence, and one sentence from you would get them in. I've said some of these sentences before and regretted them later, so now there's a short list I keep out of the invite emails and the calls.
 "Free forever." Early users getting it free for a while is fine. Forever is a long time, and you don't know yet what a user costs you. What I say instead: free during early access, and I'll tell you the price at least a few weeks before it ends.
 A founding price "for life" with no details. I like giving early people a better price, they took the risk. But "for life" without saying which plan, which limits and what happens if they downgrade is a future argument. If I offer it, I write it down: this price, this plan, as long as you stay subscribed.  A date for a feature they asked for. "That's coming in two weeks" gets a yes today and an annoyed email in three weeks. I say "it's on the list, here is why it's not next" or I don't mention it at all. If it ships, they hear about it first.
 Building something just for them. If one person needs a custom thing to sign up, they're probably not the user I'm building for yet. I'd rather lose that signup than spend a week on a feature only they use, then maintain it for months.
 The funny thing is people seem fine with the honest version. "No dates, but I read every message and the price won't surprise you" sounds less exciting, but nobody has to be disappointed later. And early-access people talk to each other, so one broken promise gets around fast.

 My early-access welcome email had six links in it. Now it has one 
Small confession about my own onboarding. The first welcome email I wrote for early-access people had six links. Docs, a getting-started video, the changelog, a feedback form, a community link and finally the app itself, near the bottom.
 I thought that was being helpful. Looking back it was me being nervous and throwing everything at them, hoping something sticks. If you give someone six things to click, the most likely outcome is they click nothing and tell themselves they'll come back later. Later doesn't come.
 The rule I use now: an early-access welcome email gets one link, and it goes straight to the one action that shows the product working. Not the dashboard. The action.
 How I pick that one action, roughly:
 what's the first thing a user does that makes them go "oh, ok, that's useful"? For a scheduling tool it's sending one real booking link, for an analytics tool it's seeing their own first chart
can I deep link to it, with as little setup in front of it as possible? Ideally the link lands them on that screen with an example already filled in
can they do it in under five minutes? If not, the action is too big and I split it
Worked example for a made-up invoice tool. Old email: welcome, here's the docs, here's the video, join the community, give feedback, open the app. New email:
 "You're in. The one thing worth doing first is sending yourself a test invoice, it takes about two minutes and you'll see exactly what your customer gets. [Send a test invoice]. If anything is confusing, just hit reply, it comes to me." 
 That's it. The reply-to is the feedback form. The docs and changelog go into a second email two or three days later, and only for people who actually did the first action. People who didn't get a short nudge about that same one action instead, not a new list of things.
 What I'd avoid:
 a "getting started" checklist with eight steps on day one
linking to a community before there's anyone in it
asking for feedback before they've used anything, there's nothing to give feedback on yet

 I tell early-access people the real batch size, even when the number is small 
A lot of early-access pages say "limited spots" and never say how limited. I get the instinct, a small number feels a bit embarrassing. But I've stopped hiding it. My rule now is that the invite email and the waitlist page both say the actual batch size, how many people are still waiting, and roughly when the next batch opens.
 Why I think the real number works better than vague scarcity:
 "limited spots" with no number reads like marketing, and people on waitlists have seen it a hundred times. A real number like 15 reads like an actual person deciding how many people he can support properly.
it sets the expectation of attention. If you're one of 15, you expect the founder to reply to you. That's true, and it's the main thing early users get that later users won't.
the people who didn't get in stop guessing. If they know there are 120 ahead of them and batches go out every few weeks, they can decide to wait or leave. Silence makes them assume the product is dead.
Worked example, numbers made up to show the shape. Say the waitlist has 140 people and batch two is 18 seats. The invite email to the 18 says something like:
 "You're one of 18 people in batch two. There are about 120 still on the list. I picked this batch because you all said you do X weekly, which is the thing I want to get right first. I'll reply to everything myself, so please do tell me what breaks." 
 And the 120 who didn't get in get a short note too:
 "Batch two went out today, 18 people. You're still on the list. Next batch is planned for roughly three weeks from now, and it'll be bigger if this one goes ok. If you want out, reply and I'll remove you." 
 That second email is the one most of us skip, and it's the one that keeps the list from going cold.
 What I'd avoid:
 a fake counter that ticks down "spots left" when there's no real limit
a public "1,000 people waiting" number you can't back up later
a specific date for the next batch you aren't sure of. "Roughly three weeks" is fine, a date you then miss is worse than no date
The odd side effect is it forces you to actually decide the batch size before you send, instead of inviting whoever and hoping. Picking who goes in which batch is its own thing, and there's a decent rubric for it in how to decide who gets into early access and who should wait on the EarlyHunt blog.

Every few weeks someone asks if it's worth paying to skip the Uneed queue. The free line can take weeks, skipping it is about $29.99, so it gets treated as a $30 yes or no.

 The real cost isn't the $30, it's your launch date. Say you planned a proper launch week. Quiet soft launch Monday, Product Hunt Tuesday, newsletter Thursday.  Daily. Product Hunt (resets 12:01am Pacific), Uneed, Fazier, Aura++ (8:00am UTC). One day on the homepage, so you have to be there for it.

 Three runway numbers I'd want written down before quitting a job to go indie 
I'm close to going full time on my own stuff, so runway math has been on my mind a lot this month. The thing I noticed is that "how many months do I have" is the question everyone asks, and it's the least useful one on its own. These are the three numbers I'd want on paper before handing in notice.
 1. Months left at today's burn. The simple one. Cash divided by monthly net burn, where net burn is expenses minus whatever revenue is already coming in. With example numbers, $48,000 in the bank and $8,000 a month out is 6 months. Fine as a starting point, but it assumes nothing changes, and something always changes.
 2. Months left if burn creeps up. Going indie almost always means a few new monthly costs: health insurance, tools you used to get free at work, a coworking desk, maybe ads. Same example, but burn grows 5% a month, and the 6 months becomes about 5.4. Not dramatic, but that half month is exactly when you'd be waiting on a first big customer.
 3. The most I can spend per month and still reach month 12. This is the one I find most useful, because it turns runway into a budget. Flip the question: if I want 12 months no matter what, what's my max burn? $48,000 over 12 months is $4,000 a month flat. If costs creep 3% a month, the max starting burn drops to about $3,382. That's a number you can actually check your bank statement against every month.
 I put this math into a free runway calculator on IndieHunt . It does months left from cash and burn, an optional monthly burn change with a month by month table, and the reverse mode for max burn over N months. The formulas are written on the page, and it runs in your browser so nothing you type gets uploaded.

Yesterday I added a small free domain name checker to IndieHunt. You type a startup name and it checks six endings: .com, .io, .co, .app, .dev and .ai. No signup.
 The part I want to talk about is the honest answer it gives for two of those six. When you check a name, .io and .co come back as "Can't check via RDAP". Not available, not taken. Just can't check.
 Quick background on why. The checker uses RDAP, which is basically the modern structured version of WHOIS. IANA publishes a bootstrap file that says which RDAP server handles which ending. The tool loads that, and for each ending it asks that registry's server about the name. If the server says 404, the name is likely available. If it says 200, it's registered, and you often get the registrar and the registration date too. A timeout or anything else, it says it couldn't check.
 And .io and .co simply don't have an RDAP server in that bootstrap file. So there's nothing reliable to ask.
 A lot of domain checkers will still show you a green tick or a red cross for those endings. I don't know exactly how each one does it, but if there's no source to ask, the answer is coming from somewhere else, maybe a registrar search, maybe a guess. I didn't want to ship a guess, so it says so instead. Same reason the launch stats pages say "Not tracked yet" instead of a made-up number.

 google.com : registered, registrar MarkMonitor, registration date 15 Sept 1997 (straight from Verisign's RDAP server)
google.ai : registered Dec 2017
google.app : registered March 2018
google.dev : registered June 2018
google.io and google.co : Can't check via RDAP
Also worth saying: "likely available" is a strong hint, not a promise. The registrar you buy from has the final say, and a name can be reserved or premium priced even when the registry says 404.

 Preparing Aegisora for Pilot Testing: Runtime Security for AI Agents 
Preparing Aegisora for Pilot Testing
 As AI agents become more capable, the challenge is no longer just what they can do, but how to ensure they operate within clearly defined boundaries.
 That's the problem we're working to address with Aegisora , an open-source runtime security layer designed to help govern AI agent actions through policies, risk assessment, and authorization controls.
 We're now moving toward the next milestone: preparing the project for pilot testing.
 What we're working on
 Our current focus is on three core areas:
 Risk-based action handling: Categorizing agent actions into Low, Medium, and High risk levels to support more informed decisions.
Policy enforcement: Evaluating how actions can be allowed, escalated for review, or blocked according to predefined policies.
Identity and authorization: Exploring how identity, permissions, and runtime authorization can help ensure agents operate within their intended scope.
The goal is to bring these controls into realistic scenarios and evaluate how they behave when AI agents interact with tools and business workflows.
 Why this matters
 Autonomous agents introduce a different kind of security challenge. Traditional access controls are important, but they may not be sufficient when an agent can make a sequence of decisions and take actions dynamically.
 We believe security needs to be part of the execution process, rather than something considered only before deployment or after an incident.
 A runtime approach can help make decisions more predictable, give developers clearer control over agent actions, and improve visibility into how those actions are handled.
 What's next?
 We're working toward validating the approach through pilot testing. This phase will help us assess the practical behavior of our controls, identify gaps, and understand what needs to improve before broader adoption.
 We're still building, and we see this stage as an opportunity to learn from realistic use cases and from people working directly with AI systems.

 How it works (The Architecture): Instead of a binary allow/block decision, I built a third state: Asynchronous Human Escalation .
 Aegisora sits exactly between your LangChain/LangGraph agents and your internal APIs. Safe requests pass through via a fast-path in < 10ms. But if an agent tries a high-risk, ambiguous action (like DROP TABLE users or sending bulk emails), Aegisora automatically pauses the tool call and routes it to a 'Human Review Queue'. A human manager can review the reasoning trace and approve or reject it, while the agent safely waits without timing out or crashing.
 It acts as a drop-in middleware, so you don't have to rewrite your entire AI stack.
 I need your brutal feedback! The core engine is now live and open-source on GitHub. You can get it running locally in under a minute.

 Every connection counts 
Telling the story of Whaticket is a challenge — because for the same company, there were two separate starting points.
 On one timeline, there was Cássio: an entrepreneur running a hardware technical support business in Santos, Brazil, struggling to organize customer service as his team grew. The business was going well, and his mind was ready for something new. So he started building software to bring order to the chaos of conversations — what would eventually become Whaticket, in 2020.
 On another timeline, brothers Juan Luis and Raúl were working to fuel the startup ecosystem in Lima, Peru. They saw a clear gap: small and medium businesses desperately needed a simple CRM. Marketing experts by trade, they dove into open-source technology — adapting, learning, and selling solutions to companies who needed them most, in 2021.
 After some turns and crossroads, these two paths converged around a shared mission: sustain and grow the technology Cássio had built, now with 100+ prospects energized by Juan and Raúl's drive. The team needed structure. Gabriel joined to formalize the business — and Whaticket was officially born in March 2022.
 Why we exist 
 We exist because small businesses deserve the same quality of customer service infrastructure that big companies take for granted.
 We were built by people who weren't from big tech — and that turned out to be our greatest advantage. Without legacy thinking, we built something with deep respect for simplicity, clean code, and a design philosophy that goes beyond "good enough." The result: a product that is genuinely stable, accessible, and built for humans.
 We come from the open-source world — and we give back to it. We contribute monthly to OpenPledge, our codebase lives publicly on GitHub, and we have a developer dedicated full-time to open-source contribution. We believe in taking only as much as we give.
 Why people stay at Whaticket 
 Because here they find something rare: genuine respect for work-life balance, close relationships between peers and leaders, shared decision-making, and constant communication. We're not a company built on distant, money-mediated relationships. We're a group of people who genuinely care about each other — and about the businesses we serve.
 We operate with radical transparency — from casual conversations to the deliberate choice to grow without external investors, making promises we can actually keep, advancing steadily toward what our hands can actually build.
 Where we are today 
 As of April 2026: 4,300 clients. 36 team members. ~$5M ARR .
 Not because we chased vanity metrics — but because we stayed true to what we set out to build: something simple, reliable, innovative, and genuinely useful.
 That's Whaticket .

While we love our self-serve customers and the number of accounts is growing quickly, we see an opportunity to move a little bit more up-market and serve larger teams. To do this, we are investing in the following activities. We’d love your feedback on whether this makes sense or how you think we can accomplish this.
Investment #1: Establishing an industry conference: The Browser Conference
Justification: Our product enables engineers to automate different tasks with a browser programmatically. Up until 7 years ago, engineers only had Selenium which was purpose built for front-end testing and validation. Today, we have an explosion of tools and frameworks that are tailored to what developers want to get out of modern browsers.
With that being said, we think there is plenty of end-user browser awareness for a wide audience, but there is relatively little for developers automating tasks.
The space is exploding with new libraries and technologies so it’s hard to keep up with. Many libraries commonly appear in the trending repositories:

These tools have fundamentally transformed the web automation space. New libraries and technologies are faster, lighter on network bandwidth, and more robust. Things like using 3rd party proxies, GPUs, dynamic and hybrid automation are starting to become easier and common. With further advancements in this space automating a web browser might even become easier soon than manually doing it yourself given that developers effectively have back-end control on what’s going on.

Highlight best practices, common issues, and lessons learned.

Repeated Virality: Our Growth Hack Equation
This article explores how Rezi is able to quickly acquire a large number of new users through intentionally designed processes.
By definition, this is growth hacking. From Wikipedia:
The goal of growth hacking strategies is generally to acquire as many users or customers as possible while spending as little as possible.
For many early-stage companies, paid user acquisition is not economical. As a result, rapid growth is out of reach. However, I hope to share our growth insights as they may be useful in how you think about the development, design, and communication to overcome these challenges.
Okay, so let's jump in. Our viral equation has three parts:
Virality = Offer + Information + Distribution 
1 | The Offer
What incentive does a user have to take action? The offer is what you are giving away. In our case, it is Rezi Lifetime , a digital, one-time, expensive subscription that allows users full access to Rezi features and all future updates.
The offer might have some definite characteristics: 
No marginal cost
High monetary & practical value - expensive & useful
Low effort to understand the value - reduced cognitive load
1.a | Building The Offer
Considerable thought must go into the user's experience of redeeming the offer. The goal here is to remove redemption friction.
The redemption process might have some definite frictions: 
Authentication - account creation is unavoidable so don't worry about this. Users will expect to create an account
Code Redemption - read more below
1.b | Redeeming The Offer 
In our case - the offer can either be redeemed with a coupon code or redemption code - both result in Rezi Lifetime at no cost.
Coupon code : the coupon code requires applying a 100% discount and paying for a 0$ product which requires a card to upgrade. From our experiences - users will be enraged about this and virality will not happen. Public user feedback will be negative rather than positive - instead of "Thank you it worked!" potential users will see "This is a scam, they just want your card info".
Redemption code: conversely, the redemption activates the offer without the need for a card. We'll keep those details a secret for now. Here's how easy it is to redeem an offer:
2 | The Information
The information will give the audience a place to learn about the offer.
You can partner with a deal website for this: 
You can host it yourself - I recommend Twitter since: 
It is unbiasedly democratic and interactive - users can see how others feel about the offer and choose to share the offer
It is familiar - the destination URL ( https://twitter.com ) is 100% trusted
It is simple - the character limit forces simplification
3 | The Distribution
The goal for distribution is to start a controlled conversation about the offer in a targeted and relevant online community. Be on standby to answer any questions or clear up misconceptions that could detract from a positive result.
Once you identify which online community you'd like to use to distribute the information, make the post yourself.
Questions to consider:
Does this growth process apply to what you're doing?
Is it economical to give away your product?
Can you support thousands of new users?
That's all for now 🙏🏻

0 to 50,000 Users: A Candid Look Into Creative Growth

Scaling a startup is hard. An endlessly-deep black vacuum of marketing dollars, aka paid marketing, tends to be a disgustingly expensive experiment for inexperienced marketing teams.
We've heard and criticized the motto "If you build it, they will come" objecting how vital marketing is to any organization.
While I fervently agree with this - I also like to acknowledge that we suck at marketing. So how do we manage to grow? Let's find out. Use this article to explore, learn, discover, or be inspired by our unique approach to growth.
Before going further - let's lay the groundwork to understand the perspective of the article - the characteristics of a product massively influence the economics of scaling up. In our case, we are a consumer-focused free resume software built to be used by everyone. The only two frictions for user adoption are knowing about it and a desire to use it. Unfortunately, this also means many marketing channels with high CPA (cost per acquisition) are not economical.
This article gives a candid look into the growth levers at Rezi categorized across 3 strategies:
Development Driven Growth
Partner Driven Growth
Organic Growth
1 | Development Driven Growth
If we're connected on Linkedin - you know this already, but Rezi launches a shit ton of new features. Our development is almost entirely lead by the marriage of the feedback from Rezi users and Rezi's knowledge of the resume which come together to reach the final goal of creating a resume. Precisely as it should be.
When we launched Rezi, there were none of the key features that we have today including; AI Keyword Targeting, Real-Time Content Analysis, multiple resume formats & download types, link sharing, starter templates, video guides, and more.
The idea of development lead growth should extend further past the "more features" approach as we look at the market from the enterprise lense. Fortuitously, we developed Rezi in a module way that allows for white-label deployments without much headache.
In April, we launched a Resume Management System (RMS) to bring organizations the ability to assist their users with the same proven resume experience as our users.
Here is what this looks like in practice - Universities in Korea cannot provide their bilingual students with any level of resume education or services that match our RMS's quality and price. From a CEO's, that's a beautiful thing.
To drive user adoption in Korea - deployments of our RMS have proven to be a hyper-targeted and effective way to reach our desired market (without ad spend). Seoul National University is our first paying client which is a reasonably significant achievement considering the institution's notoriety and the difficulties of selling software to a university.
Instead of Rezi marketing directly to students - the university recommends Rezi to the students.
This is the B2B2C model. A B2B2C is a particular business model where a company, rather than accessing the consumer market directly, does that via a partnership with another organization. Yet the final consumers will recognize the brand or the service provided by the B2B2C.
Roughly 5% or 2,500 users come from B2B2C RMS deployments.
2 | Partner Driven Growth
We suck at marketing, but a lot of other companies don't. Two companies that have their marketing down to a pure science are AppSumo & StackCommerce. Since January 2020 (StackCommerce) and April 2020 (AppSumo), both have joined Rezi as marketing partners. Each is worth mentioning considering their respective approach to marketing and their incentive for doing so.
In basic terms, AppSumo is a deal website that sells cool software.
To facilitate these deals, AppSumo partners with startups that are willing to offer their products and services at highly discounted rates.
To make it worthwhile, AppSumo distributes information about each deal to its vast online audience to quickly facilitate a large number of sales.
When we reached out to AppSumo - 6 million people had just lost their jobs due to COVID-19. Giving away Rezi Lifetime at no cost was ultimately the agreement we quickly came to considering the number of displaced job seekers and the sensitive timing of forecasted demands.
Where AppSump shines is their execution in communicating the value of the software. For the first time, we had external and unbiased experts speak about Rezi in a way that we had never previously done before.
3 | Organic Growth
Rezi was founded in 2015 to sell hiring system optimized resume templates and resume reviews. If we had focused on organic search, there's no telling what our traffic would be these days; however, I imagine it would be a couple of orders of magnitude higher than it is today.
I should be fired for wasting a 5-year head start on all search terms related to the resume.
Without digressing too much - the number one keyword that all resume companies are racing to rank for is "Resume Builder." It is such a high volume keyword that it kills innovation; many of our competitors copy reads the same. "Blah, Blah, Resume Builder" - however, this dreary, thoughtless, corporate strategy does work.
To escape the "resume-builder" circus above - we turned to our focus to mirror the product messaging that brought our partners the most success. Mainly focusing on the unique feature of how Rezi uses (simple) AI to create a significant advantage by optimizing content with potential keywords found in the job description.

 Viral on Reddit: The consequences of 30,756 upvotes and 47,611 visitors in 10 hours.
This is a post-mortem write up on the effect of Rezi unexpectedly going viral on Reddit starting on the morning of Friday, November 14th.
Product Hunt is a website that lists new products for people to upvote creating a curated list of the day's coolest software launches. It's pretty popular too. If you get to the top of the list you'll be the product of the day, just for 24 hours, and seen by thousands.
When I was researching best practices, I came across multiple articles that shared the story of companies that planned their launch down to the hour... months in advanced. Rezi was no different. From the carefully designed product-photos and expertly-animated explainer video to the email we sent out to past users, every detail was considered.
We shuffled to the office at 7pm KST and launched Rezi at 2am PST - just two 2 hours into the day so we could maximize our launch's exposure. We anxiously watched as nothing really happened (lol). Rezi just stagnated in the middle of the day's list of 20 or so products... pretty disappointing considering the effort. Yet the team was in the office and ready to stay up all night to support the launch.
By the end of the 24th hour, approximately 245 people signup for Rezi. Worthless.
Let's go back to around 11pm, about 4 hours into the plodding Product Hunt launch - I figured since I was going to be awake all night, it as a great time to do an improvised AMA on Reddit - an AMA (Ask Me Anything) a conversation where you list what is unique about yourself and people get to ask questions about you. It's a hugely popular community with over 20 million subscribers. From A-list celebrities to Barack Obama, this subreddit pulls some big names and often blows up to huge threads & tens-of-thousands of upvotes considering it is conversation-based unlike other picture-based subreddits.
Typically, I try to do one small AMA for the Korea subreddit once a year to talk about being a leading startup in Korea... But since it was launch night, I decided to talk about something else - the founding story of Rezi and how it led to the creation of our new software:
"When I graduated college, I had interviews at Google, Dropbox, Goldman Sachs, and others because of my resume, despite a 2.2 GPA. Now we've build a software to make the same resume for free. AMA!"
What happens next is every marketer's wet dream - the conversation went nuclear.
Here are the consequences of going viral on Reddit:
• 30,756 upvotes and 3,128 comments
• Reddit flooded Rezi with a torrential flow of about 500 users at any given time
• 47,611 visitors landed on the Rezi website
• 7,239 created a Rezi account. 3,844 created an anonymous guest Rezi account
By the end of the day, 30,756 upvotes and 3,128 comments later, My ad-libbed AMA was at the top of the 20,000,000 subscriber Subreddit for about 8 hours (take that Product Hunt!).
Unfortunately, I don't know how many people read the AMA but I do know how many people visited Rezi as well as the number of people who signed up for a Rezi account.
For approximately 12 hours straight, Reddit flooded Rezi with a torrential flow of about 500 users at any given time.
By the end of the day, 47,611 visitors landed on the Rezi website. An absurd amount compared to the usual 90 - 250 daily visitors when we aren't actively marketing anything.
Of these 47,611 visitors, 7,239 created a Rezi account. 3,844 created an anonymous guest account. You can see the effects on our growth graph in the admin below.
Here are my after-thoughts categorized by what went right, what went wrong, and what I learned.
What went right:
• I posted very early on a slow morning with no interesting AMAs. The moderator of the AMA subreddit gave my post a badge which almost immediately which resulted in more attention.
• The tone-setting first question was about user privacy - The answer was well received (We don't sell user data in any capacity).
• Handled critical comments well and without provoking more negativity.
What went wrong (a lot):
• Reddit is known to be strictly anti-promotion and many users thought that this was a paid post.
• I had linked to the wrong image of the resume and as a result many people dismissed my knowledge of a resume and criticized the effectiveness of the software.
• In the early hours of the morning (3-7am) I made a ton of typos and gave such tired answers that some questioned my English speaking abilities (lol again).
• Product Hunt
What I learned:
• A result like this is not repeatable. This will absolutely never happen again and the same result would cost thousands of dollars in marketing budget. I am very grateful for the coincidences that lead to the success of the post.
• Users love Rezi.
• The vocal minority of Reddit is incredibly charged, suspicious, and accusatory of ill-intent.
Well, that's about all I have to say.
Thanks for reading.

 I built a visual twin of Shopify stores to find where customers get stuck 
I’ve been working on something called StoreTwin .
 The idea came from doing Shopify CRO and technical SEO work at Shugert.
 When we audit a store, we normally bounce between analytics, crawling tools, the storefront, navigation, collection pages, product pages, and a bunch of spreadsheets trying to answer a simple question:
 What path is the customer actually taking, and where is the store making that path harder than it needs to be? 
 So I started building a different way to look at it.
 StoreTwin takes a public Shopify URL and creates an interactive visual twin of the storefront.
 It:
 discovers the store structure and connections between pages
maps likely shopper journeys
lets you explore the store visually instead of as a list of URLs
uses GPT-6 Astra to investigate a specific friction point
proposes a possible improvement
lets you replay the current journey vs. the proposed one before touching the live store
The important part for me is that the AI isn’t just producing a generic CRO audit.
 It has the actual structure of the store as context and is supposed to investigate one evidence-backed opportunity at a time.
 Right now it’s still an MVP.
 There’s no Shopify write access, billing, or complicated onboarding. You give it a public Shopify store and it builds the twin.
 I initially built it as an internal tool for our agency, but while working on it I started wondering if this could be useful as a standalone product for merchants, ecommerce teams, and other agencies.
 I’d especially love feedback from people here who work with ecommerce:
 Would you use something like this before making CRO/UX changes to a store? 
 And what would be more valuable to you: finding problems, simulating fixes, or being able to compare customer journeys before and after a change?

September 7, 2026 
 For years, I treated small Shopify development requests as the least interesting part of agency work. They were the tasks that sat between l 
For years, I treated small Shopify development requests as the least interesting part of agency work. They were the tasks that sat between larger projects: fixing a Liquid bug, changing a product page component, cleaning up structured data, removing a script that was slowing down the storefront, adjusting a collection template, or implementing a small CRO idea that had already been approved internally.
 Most of these changes were not technically difficult. An experienced Shopify developer could often complete the actual implementation in a few hours. What took me longer to understand was that the technical work was rarely the real problem. The larger issue was that the traditional agency model is not particularly efficient when the client already knows exactly what needs to be changed.
 At Shugert, we still work on the kind of projects that genuinely benefit from an agency structure: migrations, complex integrations, technical SEO, custom development, performance work, and anything where there is real ambiguity around architecture or implementation. Those projects justify senior involvement because the cost of making the wrong decision can be much higher than the cost of writing the code.
 Small tasks behave differently.
 If a merchant wants a component moved above the buy button, a field added to Product schema, or an approved design implemented in a theme, the outcome is already clear. The work may still pass through intake, review, estimation, scheduling, QA, and client communication, but the surrounding process can easily become larger than the implementation itself.
 That is when a simple technical request starts to look like a business-model problem.
 Retainers solve some of this, especially for merchants with a steady stream of SEO, CRO, performance, and engineering work. But there is another type of Shopify merchant that does not need a full agency team every month and still has a meaningful backlog of changes that should be shipped.
 These are usually not emergencies. They are small improvements that sit in the uncomfortable middle between “important enough to matter” and “urgent enough to force action.” A schema issue can wait. A small performance problem can wait. A PDP improvement can wait. A tracking fix can wait. A collection template can wait.
 The store keeps working, so the backlog keeps growing.
 Over time, those tasks stop looking small in aggregate. They create technical debt, slow down merchandising, leave CRO ideas unimplemented, and make the storefront harder to improve. The merchant may not need another large project, but they do need a better way to get routine engineering work out of the queue.
 That was the point where I stopped thinking of small Shopify development as simply cheaper agency work and started thinking of it as a separate category.
 Freelancers are an obvious answer, and for many merchants they are the right one. A good freelancer can be fast, experienced, and economical. The tradeoff is that the merchant often becomes the coordination layer. They have to find the right person, explain the context, manage access, review the result, and decide whether the change is safe.
 The quality of the process depends heavily on the individual developer and on how much technical judgment exists inside the merchant’s own team. For sophisticated ecommerce companies, that may be manageable. For everyone else, coordination becomes part of the cost.
 Then AI changed the economics of the implementation layer.
 Liquid, JavaScript, CSS, JSON templates, schema changes, and common Shopify theme patterns are increasingly easy for capable models to generate. When we started building TaskerArmy , that made code generation look like the obvious opportunity. If a merchant could describe a change and the system could produce the necessary Shopify code, it seemed like much of the friction might disappear.
 It did not.
 The merchant does not actually want code. The merchant wants the store changed safely.
 That distinction changes the product entirely.
 The hard questions are not whether a model can write a Liquid snippet. They are whether the request is clear enough to execute, whether the right theme and files are being modified, whether the change conflicts with existing customizations, how the result should be validated, what happens if publishing fails, and when the system should stop and escalate instead of continuing automatically.
 Those questions pushed us toward what we now think of as bounded engineering.
 A bounded task has a clear objective, a limited scope, and an outcome that can be validated without forcing the system to make a broad business decision. Adding a field to Product structured data is relatively bounded. Implementing an approved PDP component can be bounded. Removing an unused script is usually understandable.
 “Improve our conversion rate” is not bounded. Neither is “fix our SEO,” “migrate our ERP,” or “redesign our product experience.”
 Those are judgment problems before they are implementation problems.
 The more we work on this, the more I think the boundary matters more than the automation itself. There is a tendency in AI products to treat increasing autonomy as the goal, but an engineering system may become more useful by becoming better at recognizing what it should refuse to do.
 If a Shopify task is clear, contained, and testable, software can potentially handle much of the workflow. If the task becomes architectural, ambiguous, or commercially risky, escalation should be part of the design.
 That does not make products like TaskerArmy replacements for agencies. A better framing may be that they remove a class of work that never really needed an agency-style process in the first place.
 There is still enormous value in senior engineering for migrations, B2B implementations, complex integrations, technical SEO strategy, international architecture, and projects where the client does not yet know what the right solution should be. Using senior engineers for predictable storefront changes because there is no more efficient operating model is a different issue.
 The business model around this is still something we are figuring out.
 Hourly billing is familiar, but it keeps the customer focused on developer time. Fixed project pricing makes little sense when the “project” is a small theme change. Unlimited development subscriptions sound attractive until usage becomes unpredictable. Credits or engineering runs are easier to understand, but engineering work is still variable, so the product needs clear boundaries without recreating the same estimating machinery it was supposed to replace.
 That is what makes this category interesting to me.
 The opportunity may not be simply to make development cheaper. It may be to redesign the transaction itself.
 If a merchant can submit a clear Shopify task and trust that it will be implemented, validated, and shipped safely without turning the request into a miniature project, that begins to look like a different kind of service.
 It is not conventional SaaS because the customer is buying an outcome more than a tool. It is not really an agency because many tasks should not need a project team. It is not a freelancer marketplace because the merchant should not have to coordinate individual developers. It is not fully autonomous software because there are still cases where human engineering judgment is essential.
 I am not sure the category name matters much yet.
 What matters is whether the economics work and whether merchants trust the workflow enough to use it.
 After years of watching Shopify backlogs grow for reasons that have very little to do with the difficulty of writing code, I am increasingly convinced there is a real problem here. The interesting question is no longer whether AI can generate Shopify code. That part is becoming ordinary.
 The harder question is whether we can build an operating model around that capability that is cheaper than traditional development, safer than blindly generating code, and simple enough that merchants actually use it.
 That is what we are trying to figure out.
 If you run an agency, manage a Shopify store, or have tried productizing technical services, I would be interested in where you draw the line between work that can be standardized and work that still needs senior human judgment.
 We’re still early, and part of the reason I’m writing about this publicly is to keep the experiment honest. TaskerArmy is also listed on TrustMRR where the revenue is independently verified through Stripe.

 Integrating our Service with Addons.io 
Addons.io
QuotaGuard grew out of the Heroku eco-system starting wayyyyy back in 2013. Since then, Heroku has seen a lot of, shall we say, "changes"? Yea, "changes" is a good word.
One thing that we absolutely love about Heroku is the easy of use, especially setting up Add-on's for the marketplace. Since we've integrated with IBM Cloud ( what a gawd-awful cloud platform : do not recommend ), AWS, Azure, GCP, Render, and a few others, we're pretty attuned to how easy a marketplace is to integrate with and how much trouble it is for service to hitch into their eco-system.
Recently we started working with some other Heroku add-on service providers that were trying to simplify this process by taking all the good of the Heroku design, but making it plug-and-play for other platforms-as-a-service companies.
That's how we started working with Addons.io in the past month. We're trying to complete integrating our service into their platform to see where they can take it going forward.
The real goal would be for any Indie Hacker with a software/SaaS service that a platform's customers would need (db's, logging tools, network tools, security tools, etc) to hook into Addons.io and instantly be available on all sorts of PaaS's, like Render, Fly.io , AWS, Gigalixir, etc.
If this works, I'll make sure to write up a more formal experience document for other Indie Hackers in case Addons.io might be a good fit for them.
So far I'm impressed and they seem to have a really good start...
stay tuned...

It's Microsoft, so I don't think anyone would be surprised if I said that "there are a lot of issues with their procedures and technical documentation". If that's a surprise, I'd love to know what Microsoft products you're using.
We did find it stunning how much of Azure's marketplace onboarding technical documentation was just flat out incorrect. Usually you can find an error and say "oh, I see this likely was something it use to do, but this value has changed a little bit, no big deal..." but that's not the level of incorrectness in Azure's documentation. In the end, we just worked against the Azure API as a blackbox and figured out how to integrate with user sign ups, plan changes, usage, and cancellations by blind testing. Once we had that all figured out, there's not much more integration that needs to be done from a technical standpoint.

 July Pandemic Update - Very Boring and I like it! 
July 2020 continued to demonstrate the same overall trends I’ve seen in the last few months for QG. From my vantage point, very little changed in the overall business environment for cloud application service providers.
The most obvious takeaway was there was nothing abnormal about the month, it was boring, routine, and predictable. In 2020, that's a welcome sign.
We experienced normal subscription growth in June and, once again, I didn’t notice any lingering effects from the pandemic although I continue to keep my eyes open for any signs of a slow down.
As businesses continue to migrate towards a new normal, it seems many enterprise customers have their work from home teams established and are moving forward with normal business operations, to include using cloud infrastructure services.
Pent-Up Bounce Back?
Now that we're well into the new normal, I am starting to wonder...will there be an IT infrastructure spending boost in the future as the pandemic becomes less of a threat and the future looks more positive?
Since many companies still aren't operating with completely back-to-normal budgeting, plans, or operations, this may be wishful thinking or too far off to assume will come to fruition, but it is something I've been thinking about a little bit lately.
That's a lot better than the "how bad can this get" thinking of just a few weeks ago.
Hopefully, there is a delayed spending boost to come at some point in the future. It could be six months out, or it could be two years from now. But once the rear-view mirror sees more pandemic that I do out my front window, I'm starting to believe that a delayed cloud infrastructure spending boom is a possibility.
Check back in again in August!

 April - June Coronavirus Update

That certainly removes a level of stress and uncertainty about the future and instills confidence that the main mission of QG can continue well into the future.
Most customers that I speak with appear to indicate the same sentiments, one where now that everyone has transitioned to a reliable WFH setup - that appears likely to continue for the foreseeable future - enterprise-level corporate projects continue to be initiated, expanding, and growing.

 End of March Coronavirus Results 
Obviously, it's been a busy few weeks. But I wanted to update on how QG was doing in light of roughly 2-3 weeks of global economic shutdowns across a majority of our customer base.
Similar to last update, nobody has written us noting that something needed to be changed due to the business environment. Mostly, as far as we seen, it's business as normal.
There have been a few retail customers that have downgraded as a result of slowing business, but that has been manageable for the month, so far. We aren't seeing cost cutting at a level that would cause me concern at this phase of the pandemic.
Sign ups continue at a normal, to slightly accelerated, pace. As QG is part of the cloud infrastructure, we may be benefiting more from the overall increased need for cloud services that is occurring from businesses moving to WFH across the globe.
With these updates, I'm going to try and make sure to pass along any tidbits that I think could help an IH'er in the future with product ideas, generation, or production.
First Tidbit : Fortunately, the IT departments for our vendors and customers continue working and we haven't seen anyone indicate they can't help or respond EVEN through their customer-facing business is closed.
If you're trying to think of a product to make, having a product or service that is integrated into an IT department is a good idea, as IT never closes (even if the Internet is down for days, IT will be working...). No matter what is happening in the world, tools used by IT departments are likely to continue to be needed and/or increased during periodic changes to normal business operations.

 First Weeks of Coronavirus Quarantine Results 
I'm pretty sure a lot of people learned a lot about how stable, necessary, and vulnerable their business's were in the past 2+ weeks in the USA and Europe.
I also did not know how vital QuotaGuard would be for my customers in the face of a pandemic, but it's been a few weeks and I can report based on what I've learned so far from customer activity.
First of all, not a single customer has written us using any variation of the phrase "because of the pandemic, we are..." which is surprising. If you look at Customer Service emails over the past month, you would have no idea anything had changed.
At this point, we haven't seen a dramatic drop off in sign ups or any disappearing acts from current users. For mid-way through the month, we're down about 0.5% in MRR (mainly due to one customer wrapping up a project), which is sometimes typical, as MRR growth usually occurs in the latter half of a month for QuotaGuard. This is due to customers exceeding usage limits and upgrading as the month progresses. Most of the early part of the month, MRR decreases when a few customers cancel and/or downgrade. I try hard not to look at numbers before the 15th of each month to keep my spirits up. But this month, of course, I made an exception.
Only time will tell if this stable to slightly positive trend continues, or if worse weather is in the future.
If a national lock-down occurs, will customers cut off "in progress" projects and cancel current subscriptions...possibly to pick them up again in the future? Or will most tech companies (by far our biggest customer segment) continue to work, deploy, and create new projects from remote locations?
I'll post any new changes I observe to share how QuotaGuard is seeing the market shifts as a result of the pandemic and the human/business reactions to the situation.
Stay safe out there everyone.

To reach this point, a lot of work had to be done to the website to marry the two parallel, but different, product offerings and distinguish one from the other both in Features and Pricing.
Personally, I find it a challenge to sell two different products that both, at their core, solve the same problem...one just has a more robust security implementation and is run on a more secure infrastructure for customers that need a higher level of security.
The logical question is, "why not just make the more secure option an "add-on" type of bolt-on, where a customer could select at checkout that they want the most secure version of the product, instead of make it two separate purchase choices?"
Unfortunately, the two are not interchangeable, they are built on two different server setups and a customer can't just switch from one to the other seamlessly. Therefore, we have to market them as two different products that need to sold independently from each other. That has made marketing and the pricing page a bit tricky to present successfully.

 Successful and Exciting First Year 
Taking over a project of this scale can be daunting and...well, scary to be honest. Nobody wants to mess up anything that's already working. To be honest, I've had a lot of anxiety over the year and really had to double down on making sure we were tackling the most important and urgent projects in the most appropriate order.
We all know stories of acquiring the wrong company and your money goes poof . I knew from the start this was not one of those companies, however what if I couldn't steward the business forward and tripped us into some irrecoverable pit? This concern can lead to some sleepless nights.
By the end of the year, we could breath a little easier. We'd survived 12 months of continuous operation, passed through our first real scalability challenge, and were making daily improvements to the platform that customers requested. We'd hardened the security of the platform, instituted more through end-to-end testing, and learned more of what the Elixir community needs to succeed in their own projects.
In the end, that's what makes the business so exciting...to see the amazing projects our customers are deploying. Medical, retail, infrastructure, crypto, educational, etc.
